topic: The Origin and Color Dependence of the Index of Refraction

sections.title: Prerequisite: The Harmonic Oscillator Model
sections.content: Briefly introduce the electron as a mass attached to the nucleus by a spring (Lorentz Oscillator Model). When an electromagnetic wave hits the electron, it begins to oscillate at the frequency of the incoming light.
sections.example: Visualize an electron as a ball connected to a spring; the incident light wave acts as a driving force pushing the ball back and forth.

sections.title: Origin: Light-Matter Interaction
sections.content: Explain that the index of refraction (n) arises from the phase lag between the incident light wave and the secondary waves emitted by the oscillating electrons. This interference reduces the phase velocity of the total wave.
sections.example: Animation showing the incident wave and the 'lagging' scattered waves overlapping to create a resultant wave with a slower phase velocity.

sections.title: Mechanism: Color Dependence (Dispersion)
sections.content: Introduce resonance frequency (ω₀). As the light frequency (color) approaches the natural resonance frequency of the electron-atom system, the phase lag changes drastically, causing the index of refraction to vary with color.
sections.example: A graph showing 'n' vs. 'wavelength'. Near the resonance peak, the curve shifts sharply, illustrating why blue light (higher frequency) bends more than red light in glass.

sections.title: Visualizing Dispersion: The Rainbow Effect
sections.content: Apply the concept to a prism. Because 'n' is color-dependent, different colors experience different phase velocities, leading to different angles of refraction (Snell's Law: n₁sinθ₁ = n₂sinθ₂).
sections.example: A 'Rainbow Prism' animation: A white light beam enters a prism and splits into a spectrum, showing how each color follows a distinct path based on its unique 'n'.

sections.title: Real-World Application: Chromatic Aberration
sections.content: Summarize by linking the theory to a practical device: a camera lens. Explain that because blue and red light focus at different points, lenses must be corrected to prevent blurry, colored fringes.
sections.example: An animation of a 'Blurry vs. Sharp' image; showing how a multi-lens element system (Achromatic doublet) cancels out the color dependence to bring all colors to a single focal point.
